prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, in which many neutral atoms held at a magic wavelength reach fractional uncertainties near 10^-18

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: B001 with Katori and Ye. I have tried to separate the scientific case from the fact that six members now prefer it. The scientific case stands on its own. The distinct step is state-insensitive trapping of many neutral atoms at a magic wavelength, which keeps the clock transition unperturbed while gaining statistical power the single-ion approach cannot offer. Ye's group then showed what that buys, with systematic control and coherence at the 10^-18 level and clock comparisons that other laboratories reproduce with Sr, Yb and other species. This is an invention, and the performance claim can be tested by comparing one clock against another. That fits the test I applied in 2023 and described this year, discovery or invention and not lifetime achievement, and the committee should be able to name the topic and the people responsible. Here the credited pair is two names for one idea and its decisive realisation. I do not make the case conditional on the formal redefinition of the second. The demonstrated and reproduced uncertainty is the result, and the redefinition is a metrological decision that follows later. My citation says what is new relative to 2005 and 2012, many atoms at a magic wavelength, and does not claim credit for other groups.
statement.case_against: The main reservation is unchanged. A committee can read the lattice clock as the third prize in optical frequency metrology after the 2005 frequency-comb prize and the 2012 prize for control of single quantum systems, and so as a continuation and not a new discovery. I answer that the overlap is one of lineage, not of content, but I cannot show that every colleague will accept this. Lemonde, Ido, Takamoto and the PTB, NIST and Paris groups sit outside the two names, and I have not verified the priority chronology, so my judgment on that point rests on general knowledge and on what colleagues have reported. I also opened with B013 first, and I recognise that by preferring B001 I weight maturity and clean attribution over conceptual novelty. If that weighting is wrong, B013 is the better prize. The topological-insulator line, which I consider overdue, is held back by credit and not by science.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B013 with Bistritzer, MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero, treating the prediction plus the 2018 discovery as the core, accepting that Andrei is excluded, and agreeing that the citation should rest on flat bands and correlated phases and not on the pairing mechanism.
responses.response: I agree with your scientific framing and with the decision to keep the citation off the pairing mechanism, and that is why B013 remains my first alternative. We differ on how much the Andrei exclusion costs. You treat the trio as defensible if the exclusion is stated openly. I think the committee would be leaving out someone with an experimental claim to early STM evidence of flat-band physics, and the experimental part of this prize is then carried by one group. I could move back to B013 if the committee settles the Andrei question in a way that most members accept, but that is a judgment about credit, not about whether the physics is real. On the chair's question about what would bring B013 back to first place: a clear committee view that the Andrei question has an answer, and that maturity should count for less than novelty. I do not see that view yet.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B013 for the clean theory-plus-experiment pairing and the platform with a continuous control parameter, keeps B001 as an alternative, and says B001 is the safer choice if maturity is weighted over novelty.
responses.response: Your last point is the crux for me, and I accept the way you put it. If the committee ranks novelty first, B013 can win, and I would not call that a mistake. My own weighting is different because I am an experimentalist who trusts a result more when a second laboratory can check it against an independent instrument. Clock comparisons are exactly that, whereas in twisted bilayers twist-angle disorder and device-to-device variation are part of the record, as you acknowledge. I also doubt that eight years is too early. My concern is that the open mechanism and the credit problem arrive together. If you and Eriksson tell the room that you will move to B001 should the Andrei question stay unresolved, that would help the committee.

responses.point: Pearce moved to B001 from fifth place, calls the case clean on discovery, attribution and maturity, and keeps B024 and B013 as alternatives while acknowledging that other early lattice-clock groups lie outside the supplied names.
responses.response: I agree with the structure of your argument. I would add one thing about the overlap with earlier prizes, which you list as the main reservation: it should be answered in the citation text, not only in the discussion. The wording I propose names many atoms at a magic wavelength, which separates it from the comb and from single-ion control. On the other groups, I would not claim that the two-name credit is free of cost. Someone who has checked the early Lemonde, Ido and Takamoto chronology should report it, and I cannot, so I will not claim more than I know. If a verified chronology showed that another group's contribution was equally decisive, the case for exactly two names would weaken, and I would say so.

responses.point: Johansson moved B001 from second to first, noting that it is the only candidate ranked by all eight members and that support spans several subfields, and that he should recuse himself from any decision on B029 because it falls within his own research.
responses.response: Your support across subfields is a reason to trust the scientific argument, though I do not count it as the argument. The point I want to take from your statement is the recusal. I am a Chalmers colleague of yours and I disclosed that, but I have no stake in B029, and I would regard your recusal on that candidate as appropriate and sufficient. It does not affect my view of B001, because B029 is not among my preferred or alternative ballots. I also agree with you that the pairing mechanism of twisted bilayer graphene would not appear in a citation, so that question should not be used in either direction.

responses.point: Kroll says the 2005 and 2012 prizes honoured the comb and single-ion control and that the lattice clock's distinct idea is many-atom interrogation at a magic wavelength, but he has not verified the priority chronology and discloses a doctoral stay in Hall's laboratory.
responses.response: I accept your distinction between the comb as a ruler, single-ion control, and many-atom magic-wavelength interrogation, and it is the basis of my citation. Your disclosure about Hall is the right sort of flag. I would put it as a possible tilt toward distinctness, which is why my case should be based on the content and not on lineage. I would add that neither of us, nor Lindroth, has verified the chronology, so we should state that as a shared uncertainty and not allow it to drift into agreement by repetition. My conclusion would be unchanged if a check confirmed what we recall, and weaker on two names if it did not.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will treat the lattice clock as distinct from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 prize for single-ion control. I think the content differs, but this is a judgment and not a measurement.

The priority chronology among Katori, Ye, Lemonde, Ido, Takamoto and the PTB, NIST and Paris groups. I have not verified it and have only general knowledge and my colleagues' reports to rely on, so the claim that two names are sufficient is the weakest link in my case.

Whether I weight maturity and clean attribution too heavily against the conceptual novelty of magic-angle graphene, which I ranked first in my opening ballot, and how the committee resolves Andrei's claim if B013 is chosen.
Whether the topological-insulator credit (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, Hasan, Xue, and Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang) can be settled in a way that makes B024 a serious competitor in a later year.
statement.conflict_note: No candidate-specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B001, B013 or B024. I am a Chalmers colleague of Goran Johansson, who has declared his proximity to B029 and discounted it; that is collegial and does not touch my preferred or alternative ballots. My transmission electron microscopy work, my past work with David Clarke at IBM, and my exchanges with Japanese universities have no documented tie to Katori, Ye or the other credited individuals, and I add no new disclosure since round 1.
